speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday in Vienna, Carlos Madero, the head of the Argentinian nuclear program, told the International Atomic Energy Agency that Argentina reserves the right to develop nuclear weapons. This admission makes a total mockery of Canada's bilateral Candu agreements with the junta, and underlines the hypocrisy of entering into nuclear sales agreements with military dictatorships which refuse to sign the U.N. nonproliferation treaty. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Beaches (Mr. Young):
That the government add some bite to its incessant barking about world peace and disarmament by announcing a Canadian freeze on all nuclear dealings with Argentina at the Special U.N. Session on Disarmament, and that this House offer its sincere congratulations and gratitude to the east coast longshoremen who have refused to load uranium destined for Argentina.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL GAINS TAX ON EQUITY INVESTMENT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, equity investment pessimism is pervasive in Canada. Canadians are investing their money outside Canada and in high-interestbearing bonds and certificates. This has substantively curtailed the ability to generate equity capital in Canada and has jeopardized the survival of small business in Canada because of the high cost of debt capital. A new budget is necessary to create confidence in the Canadian economy, and it must contain incentives for equity investment. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That any new budget abolish capital gains taxation on all equity investment in Canadian registered companies.

Bankrupt fish plants are throwing thousands of people out of work in east coast communities, like Georgetown, P.E.I.; Marystown, Newfoundland; Grand Manan, New Brunswick; and Weymouth, Nova Scotia. Given that the Kirby task force is investigating the long-term problems of the fishery, is the federal government planning any specific emergency measures in the interim to ensure the survival of the important fish industry and to get it back on its feet?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in areas where the fishermen do not have an alternative counter to sell their fish, we have intervened. The most recent case is St. Anthony. In other areas such as Georgetown, I have no information that leads me to believe that, in spite of the fact that it is the height of the lobster season, fishermen are having any difficulty disposing of their catch. In some cases plants are being negotiated for, and I know that in the case of Georgetown there have been contacts with the company which owns the facility. I have indicated to the provincial minister that as much as it is within my power to intervene, I will try to find a solution. There are areas where owners of plants have decided not to reopen for other reasons. A good number had expanded to the point where there was no way the supply of fish could keep them going.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The minister must be aware that the major trading countries of the world have agreed to reduce their tariffs by an average of 40 per cent over the next several years, with the inevitable result that the United States based multinationals will be even more inclined to serve Canadian markets from abroad. With unemployment levels at record highs, exactly what action is the minister and his government prepared to take to reduce plant closings and to arrest the outflow of capital which could be used to put Canadians back to work?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: QUERY RESPECTING GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO HALT CAPITAL OUTFLOW

June 9, 1982

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hope to conclude my remarks within a reasonable period of time because of course there is an over-all limit to our debate on the energy bills.
I do not want to repeat anything that I said last night, but let me just say that there can be no settlement of the offshore dispute, there can be no development of the Hibernia and Hebron oil fields off the coast of Newfoundland, until there is
a political accommodation. Let me say, Madam Speaker, that there will never be a political accommodation while we have a minister of energy, mines and resources who acts as this minister has acted.
I now refer to The Evening Telegram of Wednesday April 7, 1982, with the headline "Tory tide sweeps Newfoundland". In that paper, after the great victory of the Peckford government on April 6, the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) was asked for his comments, and I quote now from the CP story headed, "Lalonde says the Tories lied". That was the conciliatory position that the minister took after the people of Newfoundland overwhelmingly gave an endorsement to the position of the Newfoundland government on the offshore dispute. The article says:
The sweeping Conservative victory in Newfoundland's general election will not change the federal government's position in the dispute over control and management of offshore resources. Energy Minister Marc Lalonde said Tuesday.
Lalonde, accusing Premier Brian Peckford's Conservatives of resorting to "outright lies'' during the 22-day campaign, said the election results mean nothing as far as Ottawa is concerned.
"Our principles remain the same," he told reporters. "We have no new proposals to put forward."
Lalonde said the federal government held back from intervening in the campaign even though there were "a lot of misrepresentations .. . frankly outright lies" from Conservatives about the federal position on offshore resources.
Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that there is now just about a state of war between the province of Newfoundland, the last province to enter confederation, and this government here in Ottawa which thinks it can ignore the majority opinion of the people of the province of Newfoundland, developed and delivered overwhelmingly in the election of April 6? Then they have a federal minister say that the government has lied and he will not change his position whatsoever as a result of that election victory. Then they have the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), Mr. Speaker, go down to Newfoundland on May 19 and make an announcement. There is a picture of the Minister of Justice down in Newfoundland threatening the government-
Order, order.
-telling the people of Newfoundland that he was going to take this matter out of the purview of the Newfoundland courts and bring it to the courts in Ottawa. There is a picture-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I am sure the hon. member knows what I am about to indicate to him. I can keep it brief. Perhaps he can keep his remarks in the category of "tell" and not in the category of "show and tell".

1 accept your injunction, Mr. Speaker, because, of course, your rulings are known for their sagacity.
June 9, 1982

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: That's thin ice.
Oh, oh!
On the opposite side of the House we have "assidy". In the Chair we have sagacity.
Oh, oh!

That is the atmosphere. Hon. members over there can bellow and shout but it will mean that I will keep speaking all day and all night. 1 have unlimited time. Or hon. members can let me conclude my remarks because I have a few pertinent things to say.
That, Mr. Speaker, sets the background as to how the government of Newfoundland has been cheated by the government opposite in a negotiation on something that could split this country apart and which could endanger confederation as it is now in Newfoundland.
Just to put things in perspective I want to give you some economic facts. Why is it that the government of Newfoundland and the people of Newfoundland want so badly to have the administration and control of these offshore resources? 1 will tell you why, Mr. Speaker. Do you know that right now, today, the official unemployment rate in Newfoundland is 16.1 per cent? We are told there are 38,000 unemployed people in Newfoundland and the actual official rate is 17 per cent. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that the rate in reality, not the official rate, is double that? I refer you to the study done by the Economic Council of Canada in 1980. It is entitled "Newfoundland-From Dependency to Self-Reliance. On page 48 we find:
During the month of March when seasonal unemployment in Newfoundland is high, for every four individuals counted as unemployed, there may be three others with rather similar socio-economic characteristics and recent job experience who want a job but are not actively searching work.
People know there are no jobs even if they seek them. The official rate today is not 16.1 per cent. The actual unemployment rate in Newfoundland today, as sure as I am standing here, and let me be struck down if I am not telling the truth, is 32 or 33 per cent. That is why the government of Newfoundland wants to have control and administration of its own resources. That is why this is such an important matter to the people of Newfoundland.
Let me refer you to the magazine entitled Au courant. It is put out by the Economic Council of Canada. It is Volume 1, No. 2, Fall, 1980. It deals with the Newfoundland situation as well. I look now at page 4. Do not think, Mr. Speaker, and let no member opposite think, that we are lazy in Newfoundland, because Au courant reports as follows:
First, the work ethic is very much alive in Newfoundland. Compared with their Ontario counterparts, unemployed Newfoundlanders made a greater effort to find work. More than Ontarians, Newfoundlanders search for jobs outside of their own locality and even outside the province. Newfoundlanders are also more mobile than Ontarians. They are not only willing to work elsewhere in the province or outside the province, but they have proven that willingness by holding such jobs in the past.
Petroleum Administration Act
That is an excerpt from a report prepared by the Economic Council of Canada. We do not have this unemployment problem because we are lazy louts, because we are too lazy to get out of our way and because we want unemployment insurance. We want work. This government here in Ottawa is keeping us from getting work. This Liberal government is dedicated to keeping us ignorant and poor and is forcing us to continue for another 100 years looking for work everywhere on the globe. That is what this issue is about, Mr. Speaker. That was from page 4. 1 am moving on to page 9 of the same magazine.
Just listen to this, Mr. Speaker. I do not want to interrupt the cabinet meeting over there. They do not have enough decency to carry on their conversations outside.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Why don't you go to hell?
The minister of "oozlette" should go outside if he wants to have a conversation now.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: What about the other people?

Then we have the minister who is supposed to be the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Gray). Let him listen and learn of the conditions in Newfoundland. He was the one who killed the synchrolift for the Newfoundland dockyards and tried to stop employment in Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: What about your two colleagues over there?
You haven't even got the manners of an ignorant lout. Go outside if you want to talk.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Two of your colleagues are talking. That is how important you are in your own party. They do not even listen to you.
Oh, oh!
Mr. Speaker, if I thought that minister had a contribution to make to anything, I would sit down and let him speak. He never speaks in this House. He oozes. That is all he ever does in this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Just listen to him.

The minister responsible for the Post Office should keep his mouth shut.
On page 9 of Au courant we find the following:
Ul benefits in the province amount to $408 for every Newfoundlander; the comparable figure for all Canada is $169. A scant one-fortieth of personal income in Canada comes from unemployment insurance; in Newfoundland, UI is the source of one twelfth of personal income.
Do you understand that, Mr. Speaker, that in my province one twelfth of all personal income comes from unemployment insurance? Do you think we want that condition to go on forever? The average for Canada is one fortieth, but in Newfoundland it is one twelfth. It might suit the Liberal government to believe that we are satisfied in Newfoundland with

June 9, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
unemployment insurance. But, believe me, we are not. We do not want Liberal handouts; we want work and we want the opportunity to work. We want to earn income, and that is what this struggle over the offshore is all about, because unless Newfoundland has the control and the administration of the offshore it will never have work. Our people will be like gypsies for the rest of their lives looking for work and leaving their wives and children behind.
I will quote now from a column written by Mr. Don McGil-livray of Southam News. His article is written about the report. He writes about the average earned income in 1978, and let me stress the words "earned income". His column, in part, reads:
In 1978, the average earned income for Canadians was $6,928. The comparable average income per Newfoundlander was $3,710 or 53.6 per cent of the national average.
The earned income in Newfoundland is 53 per cent of earned income for the rest of Canada. Is it any wonder that we want justice? Is it any wonder that we want opportunities? Is it any wonder that we detest the government that sits in this House and tries to keep us from being in a position where we can earn our own way and make a contribution to the rest of Canada?
Let me give you some other figures, Mr. Speaker. The per capita income in Newfoundland is two thirds of the national average. That is because of transfer payments. We are grateful, of course, to be a part of Canada and to be receiving these kinds of payments, but we do not want always to be dependent upon the rest of Canada. When we have a chance to become independent and make a contribution, why is there a government in Canada-and there is a Newfoundlander who sits in its ranks, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey), who wants to stop us from ever being independent in Newfoundland-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Tell us about the hydro corridor.
Don't open your mouth, my son, or I will have to clean you up. I have no time for you. I have bigger game than you; the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien).
Oh, oh!

Newfoundland's per capita income is two thirds of the national average. In family incomes, Newfoundlanders have 80 per cent of the national average. We are glad about that. We are glad to be part of confederation and part of the social security system. But now our turn is coming. We want our place in the sun. We want to make our contribution to Canada. We brought with us all of the wealth and the riches which the Government of Canada now wants to take and to control so that we will not have control over our own destiny and we will always be beholden to the Government of Canada. That is not good enough. It is not going to work. No courts can solve it. Only a politically reasonable settlement can solve it.
That brings me to a proposal which the Government of Newfoundland made on January 25, 1982. This proposal was never responded to by the Government of Canada. The lordly minister, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who is here today for a brief few fleeting moments, never responded to the Newfoundland proposal. I do not have time to go into it
in any great detail. But for any members who want copies of the proposal, I can provide them. This proposal was more than reasonable. The Government of Newfoundland said that it would like to receive 75 per cent of the total government oil revenues, the traditional share received by the western provinces, until its fiscal and economic situation reached the equivalent of that which pertains across Canada. When that point was reached, the federal government would take more and we would take less. In the economic formula that point would be reached when we in Newfoundland had the same national earned income and the same national unemployment rate as the rest of Canada had. Is that not fair? Are we to receive less as long as our earned income is less than the Canadian average and as long as our unemployment is worse than the Canadian average? Is there anything unfair or improper about that proposal? Of course not.
Then it went on. They wanted joint management. Newfoundland did not claim that it wanted absolute ownership and control. It suggested a seven-member joint agency in which each government would have three members, with an independent chairman and a board to administer it which could not be overridden by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who can override the Nova Scotia board whenever he wants. They wanted joint management. Joint means joint; no one is superior to the other. This is what Newfoundland suggested, but members on the government side of the House would not even respond to that reasonable suggestion.
As 1 say, I do not have the time to go into all the points. They said that they wanted legislative ratification. They wanted the question of legal ownership set aside for as long as an agreement was entered into. I should like to refer to a few other brief points in the Newfoundland proposal. I will refer to a synopsis of it now, the March 16, 1982, analysis of that proposal. At page 8 it reads:
-we wished to negotiate a broad attack on unemployment using oil as the focus.
Some people think that Premier Peckford is a bit too harsh, a bit too extreme and a bit too excitable. Well, he is harsh, extreme and excitable because he is worried and concerned about the people of Newfoundland. He wants to use the offshore to negotiate a broad attack on unemployment, using oil as the focus. I say, "Premier Peckford, carry on. Whatever the controversy or the criticism is, you are trying to do something for your own fellow Newfoundlanders to put them on their feet, so that they do not have to tip their hats or bow their heads to anyone".
At page 9 it reads:
The Province must be in a position to influence the pace and manner of development and to ensure that the traditional industries of the Province are protected.
Surely to God anyone who has gone to Scotland and has seen what happened in Aberdeen, or anyone who has gone to Norway, will know what the effects of the offshore are on the

June 9, 1982

inshore. The local government or the provincial government must be in a position to control building and to control the pace of development. They have to supply the infrastructure, the roads, the water and sewage and all these things. They have to be provided by the province. We have to protect our traditional industry, the fishery. Are we to let the fishery go just because the greedy-guts federal Government of Canada now wants to hurdle on with the development of Hibernia since the Beaufort is in trouble and the Minister of Energy has assassinated the Alsands tar sands plant, has suffocated the Cold Lake heavy oil plant and has set back the oil and gas industry in Canada by years? Are we in Newfoundland to suffer? Are we to give them control and now let them rush, no matter what happens on land in Newfoundland, to get the oil out of Hibernia? Never, it will not happen. It does not matter what legal decisions are arrived at.
At page 10 in the same document it reads:
It must be remembered that, even if an offshore agreement was signed with the federal government today, there would be no resource revenues for the province for five or six years .. . until production starts.
We are not talking about immediate wealth for Newfoundland. There is no wealth. It will be five or six years before the province will get a penny if an agreement is signed this year. The province is in dire straits financially, as are most provinces. This is no bonanza for Newfoundland. We will not rush off to the banks and start banking our money. It will be five or six years before there will be any revenue for Newfoundland, even if there were an agreement this year.
Then the document goes on to point out that every proposal advanced by the Government of Canada included federal ownership as the underlying premise. Then at page 13 it points out what the Newfoundland proposal recognized, that our earned income was only half the national average and the need for the tax burden to be reduced on Newfoundlanders. We in Newfoundland have the highest sales taxes in the country and the highest cost of living. The cost of living is 17 per cent higher. It is higher in St. John's than it is on the mainland. We have the lowest incomes and the highest cost of living. We want that changed before we reduce the revenue which should come to Newfoundland from offshore oil and gas. Also it indicated that the provincial debt should be retired. We have a very heavy debt burden.
The document went on to indicate that capital expenditures should be financed from revenue rather than from borrowing, and that the provincial income should be diversified to provide for the day when the resources run out. Is that unreasonable? No, it is not unreasonable. Revenue sharing has to be based upon equity, as was indicated on page 14.
My final quote from this document is at page 17. It reads:
In summary then, the present federal proposal is faulty because it:
(1)	has no assurance of permanence;
(2)	represents total federal control not joint management;
(3)	denies the Province a constructive partnership role;
(4)	fails to acknowledge the Province's right to a fair share in resource
revenues and offers instead a new form of welfare payment; and
Petroleum Administration Act
(5)	fails to provide a comprehensive commitment to a program of economic development based on offshore resource development.
That is what was wrong with the federal proposal.
The federal government would not respond to that proposal. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources would not respond to it. The Newfoundland Government said two things.
It wanted the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to stick to his promise to set aside the question of ownership while negotiations went on, and to set it aside if an agreement was reached.
It wanted the federal government to agree again to that, after its treachery in the SIU case. The second thing it wanted was a response from the federal government as to what was wrong with that proposal. I have the document right here. They wanted the federal government to say what was wrong with that proposal for settlement which they presented on January 25. That is all they wanted from the federal government, but the Prime Minister, in his surprise attack on May 20 when he referred this matter to the Supreme Court of Canada, ignored all that and said that they were setting down pre-conditions which he could not meet.
Let me move on to May 19. I will not get into the question of the Minister of Justice and what he did when he was asked a question on May 19. I have put down a private members motion, which I am expecting the government to call in the House shortly, about the conduct of the Minister of Justice who misled this House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: You will probably ask him to resign.

Oh, my dear friend, the Minister of Justice will never meet the challenge. He has turned pale and has run so far that we cannot even catch a glimpse of him.
I have a motion. It is the government's obligation to call this motion, which accuses the Minister of Justice of misleading the House. I will not say in what manner because we will get into a little hassle over whether or not it is parliamentary. I have asked for it to be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, and that the committee report to the House as to whether the conduct of the minister was consistent with that expected of a minister of the Crown. Unless the Minister of Justice is a complete poltroon, or unless he wants to confess that he misled the House on the day in question, I am expecting the government to vote for my motion as soon as it gives it time to be debated. Then we can put this matter to the test and see.
Speak to the bill.
I am going to speak to the bill.
Then do it now.

I do not want to speak about the Minister of Justice. He is a hopeless case. He is afraid to be here and to get involved in this debate.
I will skip the question of what went on on May 19, but on May 20 the government put out a misleading press release when it referred this matter to the Supreme Court of Canada.

June 9, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
I have a copy of the release in my hand. This copy of the release was filed in the Supreme Court of Canada registry. Never in our history, as far as I could find out, has a political document of the Minister of Justice ever been filed in the registry of the Supreme Court of Canada. It was a political insult to the Supreme Court of Canada. The docket number was 17096, and it was filed on May 20, 1982. It was a statement by the Minister of Justice on the Newfoundland offshore reference. It was a disgraceful piece of action by someone, either in the minister's department or in that registry, to put that in the docket with the notices of motions and other documents. It indicated that the Government of Canada had filed that day with the Supreme Court of Canada a reference concerning jurisdiction over seabed resources in the Hibernia area offshore Newfoundland. That was not the truth; that was an untrue statement. It is not just the Hibernia area. Everyone in the country knows the Hibernia area to mean the Hibernia oil well or the Hibernia oil field.
Also I have here an affidavit of Steven M. Millan.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Is it Mr. Speaker's intention to ask the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) to speak to Bill C-103, which does not deal with the offshore issue?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) put his intervention as a question to the Chair. I am a bit awkward about replying directly in that fashion to members who may want to question the Chair. The argument about relevance is extremely difficult. I have been paying attention to the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). I think the only thing I could say is that if he will attempt to direct his remarks toward the bill, it would probably be of assistance. But I will not find that the hon. member is not relevant.

Mr. Speaker, I know that they do not want to listen to the truth. Bill C-103 defines Canada lands. They have defined Canada lands to include the Hibernia area and all the east coast of Newfoundland and the Labrador offshore area. How can any feeble-minded twit from the government benches opposite suggest that it is not relevant for me to discuss the area that is included in Canada lands?
Hear, hear!

I should have said honourable twit.
I refer to an affidavit of Steven M. Millan, executive director of the Petroleum Directorate in Newfoundland. He has examined the order in council, and the area described in it comprises 819.9 square acres or approximately 212,000 hectares-this is for the government opposite since they only deal in hectares-and 35 square miles is the area. In that area is the Hibernia oil field, the Nautilus geological structure, the Terra Nova geological structure, the west Ben Nevis and the Ben Nevis geological structure which are all oil fields, or potential oil fields. Therefore, this is not just a reference about
the Hibernia oil field, as was pretended by the minister in his release and as was stated by the Prime Minister in his letter. They know not how to be accurate when it comes to describing the facts or telling the truth.
There are pictures of the structure, but 1 dare not show them to the House since that apparently is not in order. It is also pointed out in the affadavit that even if there was an agreement reached now it would be three to five years before all the environmental and development plans could be approved. It would be over five years before there could be any production. What is the rush? What is the hurry, in other words, for the federal government to slam-bang this into the Supreme Court of Canada when the field, at best, could not be developed for another five years? It will have a life of about 25 years from first to final production.
Incidentally, as you know-I think I mentioned this last night-it was on February 12 that Newfoundland referred this matter to the Newfoundland court of appeal. We are even given false information in the Prime Minister's statement and the minister's press release on May 20. The tissue of deceit, deception and false information clouds the whole issue. One of the questions is this: is there a precedent in the history of this mighty dominion, our confederation, or has there ever been one case or situation where the Government of Canada intervened when a provincial government made a reference to its highest provincial court? Has there ever been a case in our history when the Government of Canada, against the objections of a province, took it out of the hands of the highest provincial court of appeal and referred the case instead to the Supreme Court of Canada without the consent of that province?
I will tell you that the Library of Parliament, legal authorities working for the province of Newfoundland and other people here have not found one precedent. Did that deter this Minister of Justice? Did that deter the man who is supposed to be the fountain of our justice system? It did not. He went to a meeting of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs on May 27. In giving testimony at that meeting he stated, quite improperly and falsely, that there were precedents. He cited six or eight precedents which, he said, applied to this situation. The Leader of the Government in the Senate, Senator Perrault of the other House, spoke in the other place and said there were 12 precedents. Senator Flynn of the other House had the Library of Parliament check into this. He could not believe his ears that the government was claiming that there were 12 precedents of the Government of Canada stepping in against the will of a provincial government to take a matter and refer it to the Supreme Court of Canada although it had been already before the highest court of the province. The report of the Library of Parliament was attached to the Senate Hansard of June 2. If you turn to the appendix of the Senate Hansard of June 2, you will find, on the last page called "A Critical Analysis of Reference Case Precedents", that the research branch of the Library of Parliament had considered all these cases and states:
June 9, 1982

-whether a question has been referred by the central government to the Supreme Court of Canada for adjudication while the same question or a similar question is pending on a reference before a provincial court of appeal. In addition, it is appropriate to examine the attitude of the provincial government as to whether it supported the reference by the central government, or whether it opposed it and decided to continue with its own reference before its own court of appeal.
It took every case cited by Senator Perrault and every case cited falsely to the House of Commons Justice Committee by the Minister of Justice. In every case, not one is relevant to that issue. The only case which even appears to be in the same league at all is the 1932 Radio Broadcasting Act. In that case, the matter was referred by the central government to the Supreme Court of Canada without any opposition from the province of Quebec to that reference. The reference to the Quebec court of appeal did not proceed because the Quebec government preferred to have the matter proceed to the Supreme Court of Canada.
All 12 of those references cited by the highest legal officer in this land, given to the leader of the government in the Senate to mislead the Senate, were used by him to mislead the hon. members of the House and the Justice Committee and were not precedents at all. It is unprecedented that the head of a judicial system in Canada should carry on in such a careless manner. If we suppose that he did not know that these cases were not references, he should then dismiss all of his staff who advise him. He should do that because, knowingly or not knowingly, he misled the House of Commons Justice Committee and he allowed the government leader in the Senate to do the same.
If that were not bad enough, while he was doing that he said, as recorded at page 8917 of the Justice Committee hearings, that there was a good precedent created by the prime minister of Canada, Mr. Bennett. That is the case to which 1 just referred, which is not a precedent at all.
He had this insulting remark to make about Senator Lang of the other House. Senator Lang had introduced a resolution in the other House which deplored the actions of the government in going ahead with this reference to the Supreme Court of Canada. I refer you to the Senate debates on May 20 as reported at page 4160 where Senator Lang moved a motion that the Senate deplores the decision of the Government of Canada to refer to the Supreme Court of Canada the question of jurisdiction over the seabed resources off Newfoundland called Hibernia while at the same time the appeal court of Newfoundland is seized with the matter that includes this very question.
Senator Lang is a Liberal member of the Senate, but he is a man who has a strong sense of respect for the judicial institutions of this country. He is not a toady of the Prime Minister. He is not a tame tabby or a little pussycat of the Liberal caucus. He is an independent man who moved that motion.
The Minister of Justice, who has never practised law or, if he has, it has not been for the last 17 years-just to show you the breadth and dimension of this man who heads our justice system-said, "It is evident that Senator Lang is retired. He does not work as hard as he used to because he would have
Petroleum Administration Act
found that very easy." In other words, he would have found those precedents that supported the federal action. In the first place, the precedents do not support the federal government's action. In the second place, Senator Lang is not retired. He still practises in Toronto. He has more brains, more nerve, and more gumption in his little finger than the Minister of Justice has in his whole body. If you include the rest of the cabinet, Senator Lang would be far ahead of the 34 of them put together. That is the kind of denigrating remark that this small-minded Minister of Justice made about Senator Lang because he moved this motion in the Senate. He continued with all this misleading evidence about these references, which the Library of Parliament research branch has shown to be false.
The Hon. Eugene Forsey went through all the precedents as well. I hold a list from the former Senator who finds exactly the same thing. None of those 12 precedents were relevant. None of them are on all fours with the Newfoundland case. Mr. Forsey has reviewed them, and I daresay no one will say that he is not a worker.
Senator Eric Cook of Newfoundland quit the Liberal Party because he could no longer stand for this kind of action when the federal government referred this matter to the Supreme Court of Canada. Senator Cook is one of our foremost legal luminaries in Newfoundland and is a man with more backbone and courage than any thousands of others whom I could name. He finally quit the Liberal Party because he could no longer take it. Incidentally, I heard a report of his being denigrated by one of the reporters in our press gallery who said on a radio program, "Who is Senator Cook?" "What has he ever done", this twit asked? This person from central Canada, who I doubt has ever been to Newfoundland, tried to insult Senator Cook and asked, "What does it matter whether Senator Cook had left the Liberal Party or not?" Well, what matters is this: it shows that in our Dominion there are people who believe in principle and still have the courage to carry out their principles, who are prepared to leave the party they have lived with all their lives and have supported and worked for, because they can no longer take what is happening. That takes people of courage. That takes more courage and more character than that particular cretin from the press gallery will ever exhibit. Senator Cook's resignation is a great loss to the Liberal Party of Canada, believe you me.
I know that, unfortunately, we are limited in time. I just want to make one more reference to-
Oh, oh!

You see, I do not think I have repeated myself more than once or twice in this debate. That shows how much there is to say, because 1 want to ensure that the people of Canada and hon. members of the House who care to listen understand. This is not some greedy, grasping group of people down in Newfoundland trying to take something from Canadians that it is not their right to take, or trying to keep from

June 9, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
Canadians some resources which all Canadians should share. This is a group of people in Newfoundland trying to struggle to haul themselves up by their bootstraps. Anyone who has looked at our history and seen what we have been through will realize why there was a 61 per cent vole for the Peck ford administration on April 6, and will realize what will happen to the five Liberal members who now sit in the House and have turned their backs on the people of Newfoundland while sitting here. I cannot wait for that next election to come.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Tell us about the hydro corridor.
Pardon?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Talk about standing up for Newfoundland on the hydro corridor.

The hydro transmission matter is widely understood in Newfoundland. You are trying to cut the guts out of the National Energy Board and are throwing in this little hydro clause as a sop. No one has been fooled by that, and no one thinks that hon. members opposite are friends of Newfoundland. Well, there might be a few out of the 620,000 people down in Newfoundland who think they are interested in Newfoundland.
The former Senator Forsey, who is widely regarded as a constitutional authority, said this about what the Government of Canada has done:
The Dominion government's action is, as far as 1 know, unprecedented. It is in marked contrast to the procedure that government itself followed on the patriation resolutions. It is certainly irregular. It interferes with the normal judicial procedure by virtually removing from the Newfoundland Court of Appeal an essential part of the question placed before it. It is highly improper. It is a tactic that undermines the whole judicial system.
Unfortunately, our justice system is headed by the present Minister of Justice who does not understand and who has shown by his behaviour that he is quite prepared to interfere with our court system and the judiciary whenever he thinks it is to his political advantage. He is a man who can insult and denigrate a judge and criticize him obliquely without giving it a second thought. If we had a proper Minister of Justice who had any character or backbone, this incident would never have happened.
The Newfoundland Court of Appeal has set October 6 of this fall as the date when all of the documents and factums are to be in and when it will set the date for the hearing of the issue referred to it by the Newfoundland government, which involves the whole offshore area. The issues in that case are not one bit different from the one concerning the matter which the federal government has now sent to the Supreme Court of Canada. The Supreme Court of Canada has now set the date for its hearing at November 27, I believe. In my view, it was a very bad mistake by the Supreme Court of Canada to set that matter down to be heard while the case is still before the Newfoundland Court of Appeal and a decision has not yet been rendered. They were put in a very difficult position.
Come on, wind down.

My friend to the left wants me to wind down. This is exactly what 1 am doing. They only reason I am doing that, of course, is that we agreed to a certain limited number of hours to deal with these energy bills and there are other hon. members on this side of the House who have a contribution to make.
There is no issue more important to this country than the issue I am speaking on now, because this is an issue which will not be settled for a long time yet and will not be settled unless we have a different government or see a complete change of attitude in the hon. members who sit opposite. It may, in fact, endanger our confederation unless there are changes in attitude.
So I will now wind up. 1 think I have done my best to try to explain the offshore issue to hon. members of this House.
1 will quote from an editorial in the London Free Press of May 24, 1982. It starts off by discussing whether or not the federal Minister of Justice deliberately misled the House of Commons, and said that, whether or not he did, "he certainly was less than candid." I think we can all agree with that. The editorial goes on to state:
But Crosbie is right to call for an investigation of Chretien's remarks. It would be useful for a parliamentary committee to review the standards of candour to be expected when ministers of the Crown respond to questions in the Commons.
It is very necessary to review the standards of candour to be expected when ministers of the Crown respond to questions in the Commons.
One of the most startling, highly unusual explanations of the Minister of Justice for the answer he had given to the questions on May 19 was when he said that in his mind there had been certain conditions. He now feels that whatever, is in his mind, of course, is something that he has said. He said, "There was a decision which had been made with some conditions attached. 1 just said there was no decision because some conditions had to be met". The minister said there was no decision because, although there was a decision, there were some conditions which had to be met. The standards of candour of ministers should definitely be reviewed. 1 am hoping the government will vote for my motion when it comes forward, when the government gives it time, if it has the courage to do that.
The editorial goes on to state:
As for the oil and gas court case, there is nothing illegal about the reference to the Supreme Court, but it is of questionable propriety.
That is quite right and exactly on point. At the end, in reference to the Newfoundland court, the editorial states:
Out of respect for that court and in the absence of any compelling need for a quick and definitive decision, the Trudeau government should have left the matter alone, while reserving the right to appeal an adverse ruling to the supreme court of Canada.
That is also quite right, and I highly recommend that the government rehabilitate itself in part by withdrawing the reference it has made and waiting until the Newfoundland Supreme Court deals with the matter. It should then be appealed in the normal way, to be heard in 1983, here in Canada. The government will not see any quicker development
June 9, 1982

of the Hibernia or the Hebron or any other oil field of eastern Canada by following the route it is taking. In addition to that, it has shaken the judicial system in Canada to its foundations. The government is on the wrong course. The people of Newfoundland have right and justice on their side. They want to be able to earn their own income and they want their turn in the sun. Only the kind of settlement that our party proposes for them will be the kind of settlement to settle this issue in a manner which is true to the nature of Canadian confederation. That is why it is important that this government either completely reverse itself or have the courage now to go to the electorate of Canada to see whether the people approve of the kinds of actions it has taken in the last two years and three months.

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and 1 want to thank the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) as well. I want to say at the beginning that I do not intend to match the time used by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). He said that he shed some heat on this question, and I hope I can shed some light.
I want to deal in the beginning, however, with the issue of courage because that has been raised as an essential element, courage on the part of the hon. member for St. John's West, courage in the sense of Newfoundland standing up against Canada. Canada is portrayed by the hon. member for St. John's West and other politicians in my province as being the enemy. You are courageous if you agree with the hon. member for St. John's West and the Premier of Newfoundland. However, if you hold a different position, you are somehow lacking in courage. You are considered not courageous and not standing up for your province. In my opinion, that smacks of demagoguery and I do not accept it. There are two points of
Petroleum Administration Act
view and I hope I can put the other point of view on the record today.
In terms of courage and standing up for Newfoundland, I want to ask the hon. member for St. John's West where was he standing up for Newfoundland when this government introduced in this House a bill to give Newfoundland the right to transmit hydro power across the province of Quebec to market. Where was he when that happened? That bill was put forward by a minister from Quebec and voted on by 74 Members of Parliament from Quebec from this side.
The hon. member for St. John's West took his courage in his hands and sat down for Newfoundland. That is what he did. He abstained. His party voted against it. The Conservative Party of Canada voted against the right of Newfoundland to have a hydro corridor to transmit power to market.
The hon. member for St. John's West, who talks so much about courage and for standing up for Newfoundland, sat down. He abstained. He did not vote for that. Let that be on the record. In the years to come, the record will bear out who in this House has courage, who has not, and who stands up for Newfoundland. The Government of Canada, we on this side of the House, want what is best for Newfoundland and Labrador.
This bill encourages Canadianization of the oil industry. It is a step toward self-sufficiency. We have to rely on all sources of oil if Canada is going to be self-sufficient.
I want to talk, as did the hon. member for St. John's West, about the offshore issue because it is crucial to my province at this time. 1 want to talk about the recent reference to the Supreme Court and about why there was no other option at this time but for the Government of Canada to proceed to the Supreme Court with a direct reference on ownership and the jurisdiction of those offshore resources.
There was no other option. For 14 years we tried to negotiate a settlement, a political settlement between the two levels of government. All the attempts over those 14 years failed. In order to get the matter resolved quickly, to get development going, to create jobs and revenue for Newfoundland and Labrador, if ownership is what is important, let us get it settled as quickly as possible. Let us get it settled in court.
Eventually it has to go to the Supreme Court of Canada, and a judgment has to be rendered. It does not matter what the Newfoundland court decides. Therefore, our position was to put the ownership issue in court if it was the important consideration. It can only be decided in court. I cannot decide ownership, nor can the opposition or the people of Newfoundland. Only the Supreme Court of Canada can decide ownership. The ownership issue cannot be put aside. Nobody can guarantee that the ownership issue can be put aside forever. Anybody can bring that issue to court.
A case in point is the S1U case. It was not the Government of Canada or the government of Newfoundland which brought the SIU case before the Supreme Court. It need not be a government which goes to court. Anybody can go to court. An

June 9, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
oil company can go to court and get the ownership issue decided. If that is the important issue, it can ask the court to decide.
It cannot be put aside forever. Nobody can guarantee that. At some point in time it may be decided. If that is the case, why not decide it quickly and get it out of the way?
Newfoundland has nothing to lose with this action. There are those who say that Newfoundland has a good case, that it has a unique case. They say that Newfoundland came into confederation with certain resources. I believe that Newfoundland has a unique case. If that is true, then what have they to fear in the judgment of the Supreme Court? What have they to fear in a reference to the Supreme Court? If the case is good and just, there is nothing to fear from a judgment by the courts.
If Newfoundland wins, then it has ownership and can operate as if it were Alberta. Elowever, if Newfoundland loses, it can still have a political deal. Where is the loss for Newfoundland? In this action Newfoundland is in a winning position no matter what happens. If it wins, it has ownership and can act like Alberta. If it loses, it can still make a political deal.
What is important is the deal. I do not believe that ownership is the important issue. I have never been able to understand why pure, bald legal ownership is the important issue. Let me give a case in point.
The opposition, including the hon. member for St. John's West, wants to make this government appear to be the enemy of Newfoundland and Labrador, this government which just opened up the St. Anthony fish plant in spite of the fact the Newfoundland government decided it would probably not issue a licence to that plant. That province has the highest rate of unemployment in Canada. There are 900 people out of work in St. Anthony. This government wanted to solve that problem, but it indicated it might not issue a licence. They would like us to appear to be the enemy. Are we the enemy of St. Anthony for wanting to put 900 people back to work in that community?
We were also the enemy when we created the Lower Churchill Development Corporation. Several years ago this government, this leader and this cabinet created the Lower Churchill Development Corporation, a 50-50 partnership of Canada and Newfoundland to harvest the hydro resources of the Lower Churchill River. The question of ownership is quite clear. Newfoundland owns every drop of water in that river. Who controls it? Who has jurisdiction? Who are the partners in the Lower Churchill Development Corporation? Canada and Newfoundland.
There is adequate precedent. There is no reason why the Lower Churchill Development Corporation cannot be a model for the offshore. Ownership does not have to be the overriding and overbearing issue. I do not believe that ownership is what is important. What is important is a deal, a settlement.
In that regard, I differ very little from what I heard the hon. member for St. John's West say. After you strip away all the rhetoric, all the denigration of this side, all the attempt to
make us appear to be cowards for not standing up for Newfoundland and to make this government the enemy of Newfoundland, the bottom line of what he said was that it does not matter what the Supreme Court decides. That is what I heard him say. I agree with that.
What is important is a political deal. We have a deal with British Columbia, one with Alberta, one with Saskatchewan and one with Nova Scotia. For 14 years we have been trying to get a deal with Newfoundland. We must have that deal no matter what the Supreme court decides. That is the important issue. We must have a deal with Newfoundland that is good for Canada and good for Newfoundland, a deal that will stand up over time no matter what the courts decide. That is the important line. I want to repeat it again.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) went to Newfoundland to tell the people there exactly what we were doing and why. That is what he said in his release, and that is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in his letter, that we want a deal that will stand up no matter what the courts decide.
What are the elements of that deal? For us they have not changed. Essentially there are two. The first is maximum revenues to Newfoundland, 100 per cent of the possible revenues to the government of Newfoundland. Why would we ask otherwise? Even if from a moral point of view, we should not give 100 per cent of the revenue to Newfoundland, and we should, look at the practicality. Equalization payments will flow to Newfoundland in any case. It is much better to have Newfoundland economically independent, standing on its own two feet financially. I thoroughly agree with that, as does the Government of Canada. That is why one of our principal negotiation positions has been 100 per cent of the possible revenues going to Newfoundland. What we would take out probably would be the federal corporation tax and no more. Indeed, in that settlement, Newfoundland might get more, and probably would get more than if it owned the resource, because Alberta now gets 23 per cent for a barrel of oil. Whereas in Newfoundland, if a proper deal were made, we could get more out of the deal than Alberta presently gets who owns the resource inshore.
So the first negotiating position is maximum revenues to Newfoundland. The second one is along the lines that I have already indicated, along the lines of the model of the Lower Churchill Development Corporation, that is, a joint administration. It is not Newfoundland or Canada, it is Newfoundland and Canada. We are fortunate to be part of a federation whereby we can have a government that is strong enough to help us when we need to get something developed in our province.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
We need the Government of Canada. I do not need to tell Newfoundlanders what Canada has meant to them since 1949. One of the Premiers of Newfoundland has
June 9, 1982

called confederation a blessing. That is the case, Mr. Speaker, It is not simply a matter of handouts, it is our right to expect that, it is our right to expect that Canada will help us now. And she will, if we will give her half a chance. What we want is a joint board, a joint administration on the part of Canada and Newfoundland. It does not have to be the Nova Scotia deal. In the Nova Scotia deal I understand that the power given to Nova Scotia was in the form of a veto.
No veto. Look at the agreement again.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That is a possibility. My understanding is that Nova Scotia can hold any decision up for a period of time if they do not like it. That is power, power to Nova Scotia.
Try and be truthful. There is no veto by Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: If that is not acceptable to Newfoundland, then there are other options.
Tell the truth in your speech.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: We went through the 1980 election, Mr. Speaker, and since that time, on the basis of a joint administration between Canada and Newfoundland. I do not want to talk about the details.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The minister is misleading the House. Can he point to any section in that Nova Scotia agreement that gives them a veto over decisions? The power is in the hand of the Government of Canada and the minister. The minister is misleading the House, unless he can point to a clause.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the Nova Scotia agreement 1 mentioned an option, an option.
You said "veto".

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
There are other options. Newfoundland can have its own unique deal if it so desires, a deal that will be set on that basic principle of a joint administration between Canada and Newfoundland. It does not have to be the Nova Scotia deal, it can be a different deal, a unique deal, specifically for Newfoundland. But you cannot negotiate a deal if you walk away from the table. That is exactly what happened.
We are being accused now of putting an issue in court. It was the government of Newfoundland who put that issue in court, Mr. Speaker. It was the government of Newfoundland who walked away from the negotiating table and put that issue in court. What we are saying now is, if it is in court, let us settle it as speedily as possible. We want to get back to the bargaining table because we want on this side what is best for Newfoundland. I have already cited instances of that. There is a need for oil development now in Newfoundland. It is not going to be the saviour and there will be difficulties. Let us not underestimate that. There is a direct conflict between oil and fish. Let us not paper over the difficulties that we have, let us not paper over the fears of many of our people.
Petroleum Administration Act
I know there are people with money invested who want to get going on the offshore. But there are also a lot of people in small fishing communities in Newfoundland who fear what might happen as a result of that development. That is another reason 1 think that we need the power and the support of the Government of Canada in transport, in national defence, in environmental protection, to make sure that we have the laws of both governments on our side.
There is a need to create jobs, there is a need to create wealth. My colleague to the left of me now-who was formerly the minister of regional economic expansion-has said many times that the people whom I represent are among those in Canada who need help most. They need real help, real dollars, real jobs, and the way to give them those jobs is to develop that resource. Let us get it going quickly, let us not put if off, let us not procrastinate, let us not wait for another day. There is need in Newfoundland, there is a need in Canada for that oil development. We have to have the resources in the Beaufort Sea and the resources of the Arctic and the resources offshore, if we are going to be self-sufficient. We can be self-sufficient in Canada. We have tremendous resources, if only we would stop arguing and fighting among ourselves and start working together.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
If only we could do that, Mr. Speaker. We are our own greatest enemy in that sense. We are our own greatest enemy in the sense that we have so much to be thankful for, so many resources. We continually fight among ourselves and delay the development of those resources which could bring us such great wealth and such great power and such a great economy.
So there is a need in Newfoundland, there is a need in Canada; and both those needs can be addressed and both those needs can be resolved. That is so if we can have a deal, if we can sit down at the same table and work things out, as we did on the Lower Churchill Development Corporation. We did it in Newfoundland. If we can work things out as we did in British Columbia, work things out as we did in Saskatchewan, work things out as we did in Nova Scotia, work things out as we did in Baie Verte in my province a little while ago on the asbestos mine. In that last case the government of Newfoundland and the Government of Canada sat down together at a table and worked out a deal. It is possible, it can be done, with men of good will and men of vision, Mr. Speaker. That is what has to be done with the offshore. 1 do not think we should play the game of making friends and enemies, who is for us and who is against us, who has courage and who has not. That is rhetoric. What the people of Newfoundland want now is some wisdom and some good will and an earnest desire to develop their resources for Newfoundland and for Canada. There has to be federal involvement. I would urge the government of Newfoundland to come back to the bargaining table.
The leaders of the churches in Newfoundland recently sent a telex to the Prime Minister and a telex to the Premier of

June 9, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
Newfoundland. 1 will not read the whole of it, but I will read part of it, Mr. Speaker. It says this:
-the process of negotiation is the obvious method of reconciling differences and producing some real agreement ... If this is impossible ... it is all the more important that the issues be clearly and decisively resolved by placing them before the courts of the land in some mutually agreed way.
In some mutually agreed way. If there has got to be a reference, let it be a joint reference. We asked for that. We would have preferred that, I think it is fair to say. "It is all the more important," they say. The bottom line in the telex from the leaders of the Roman Catholic Church, the United Church and the Anglican Church in Newfoundland is this:
-to enter immediately into serious and meaningful discussions on offshore jurisdiction. If as a result of such discussions they see no alternative but to put the matter before the courts, we would urge that they do this in a manner which recognizes the legitimate interests and concerns of both parties.
In other words, there is a case for Canada, there is a case for Newfoundland. In other words I think what they are saying is, and I support it-and I did not hear the hon. member for St. John's West not support it; as a matter of fact, if there was a bottom line in his speech it was exactly the same-that this can really only be solved, this offshore question, by negotiation. There really has to be a political settlement, no matter what the courts decide. I would urge Newfoundland to come back to the table, I would urge them to sit down in good faith, with some vision and with some wisdom, and strike a deal that is good for us in all parts of the country.
We do not have to choose our citizenship. I do not have to choose between being a Newfoundlander and being a Canadian. I can be both at the same time, and I can work both for my province and for my country. I think that is possible, and I think that those around that table at that time will be able to do the same thing. That is what has to be done, Mr. Speaker. I urge now that rhetoric be put aside and that all of us who really have the best interest of Newfoundland at heart come to the table and start negotiating that deal.
Hear, hear!

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I would like to ask the hon. minister a question just as he is finishing. Is the minister saying that the Government of Canada is now prepared to discuss this and to give a response to the Government of Newfoundland in connection with its proposal of January 25, 1982, which up to now it has refused to respond to? Is the minister prepared to put aside the question of ownership while the negotiations continue and if an agreement is reached? Is that what the minister is saying?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all sort of responses are possible if you are sitting at the table, if you are discussing, if you are having a conversation, if you are negotiating. All kinds of responses are possible then, but if you are not negotiating, responses become very difficult. I do not think we should be negotiating at arm's length and I do not think we should be negotiating through the media. I think if we have good will and the interests of Newfoundlanders at heart and if we come
back to the table with no pre-conditions, then there will be a response. I do not think the Government of Canada has had an opportunity to give a response.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Because there is nobody at the table to respond to. I am saying we should get back to the negotiating table. Other deals have been struck, and we could have a deal as well.

Mr. Speaker, I have chosen this occasion to speak in opposition to Bill C-103, especially because it is an example of what the government's policy is doing to the working people of Canada. In that I include Newfoundland and not least the Province of Ontario of which I represent a part, the mainly working-class riding of Spadina.
This bill deals in part with taxes in relation to the oil industry, the maritime taxes, the airline taxes, taxes for oil compensation, taxes on ownership and so on, while other bills deal with grants and huge giveaways to the richest and most powerful corporations in the world. This bill deals with the method by which the government collects billions of dollars from the working men and women of the country and hands them over to the oil companies.
All this can be illustrated by some figures covering the last two years, Mr. Speaker. In 1980 the average home burned about 4,500 litres of heating oil and would have paid about $400 for it; in 1981 that would have cost $1,170, and in March of this year it would have cost $1,275. In the same way, a family in which the breadwinner has to commute to work by automobile, in 1980 would have paid $216 for about 2,700 litres of gasoline, the following year it would have cost $945, and as of March this year it would have cost $1,030. These expenses which totalled $616 two years ago now total $2,305, so there is a difference of nearly $1,700. That comes out of the pockets of working men and women-if they are lucky enough to have a place to live and a job. In other words, the original cost of a little over $600 has more than tripled in two years.
In the over-all picture there has been a 30 per cent rise in the cost of living, all of which comes from the increase in the price of oil. This is happening at a time when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) daily tell working people to restrain their demands, not to ask for more money. They expect these people to pay 30 per cent more for necessities within two years because the government is taxing them for oil, but they are not to ask for any more money to help pay that tax. In fact, a large part of that increase in the price of oil comes from taxes.
It is interesting that Imperial Oil and its friends are putting out advertisements which, with the usual kinds of half truths, say that $3 out of every $5 of the cost of gasoline goes for taxes. That may well be true, but what Imperial oil and its friends try to hide from the working people of this country is that every cent of the taxes they pay to the federal government is returned to them, and more besides.

In the three years between 1977 and 1980 this government, and the short and unlamented government of the Conservative Party which had six months in which to make matters as much worse as it could-in tax concessions to the oil companies gave them $13 billion at a time when only $5 billion was collected from them. In other words, the giveaway by the Liberal and Conservative governments to the corporate welfare bums that are the oil companies, was $8 billion or almost $700 per worker in this country.
This year the government plans to give away much more. It was announced a couple of weeks ago that Imperial Oil and its friends would receive an extra $2 billion. The government has already taken $1.3 billion out of transfer payments to the provinces for health and education and has given it to the oil companies. In fact, what it is doing is offering the oil companies a subsidy of 80 to 93 cents on the dollar for a great deal of their exploration activities.
We have heard a lot of preaching from members on my right about how the oil companies know where to find oil, but they do not like to practise what they preach because they ask the working people to pay 80 per cent to 93 per cent of the cost of finding that oil. Then when the oil is found, using the taxes of working people, Imperial Oil and its friends to my right in this chamber, want to own the whole thing and cream off the total profit.
The whole system is now collapsing around the ears of the Prime Minister and the former prime minister, now the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark). It has been admitted by the Prime Minister and half admitted by his deputy, who has had to come back from Europe to try to hold the fort on the other side of the House that the fight against inflation was a tragic mistake. All the brave words that the Prime Minister and members on the government front benches have been spouting day after day for the last eight months were not true they now admit. This was their prime argument for enforcing misery on the working people of the country, and now they admit it was a tragic mistake. They have admitted that interest rates are too high and could go higher. They admit that bankruptcies have risen at a rate no one can remember unless they lived in the 1930s. They admit that unemployment has risen at a rate we have not heard of except in the 1930s and that all those evils are still increasing.
The government made cuts to health, education and housing and other services that working people need. It has broken promise after promise, such as the one to fund urban mass transit for the cities of Canada. This government will fund urban mass transit in New York City but not in Montreal, Toronto or Vancouver. It has admitted that factories are shutting down. We have lost about 350,000 jobs in less than a year, and the manufacturing industries which serve the Canadian people are in decline and laying off people by the tens of thousands. The government has absolutely no remedy because its only goal for the last eight months, as its members

themselves said, was to fight inflation. The government has now admitted that was a complete mistake.
The Minister of Finance claimed he was going to reduce the deficit, but it in fact has come close to doubling it since he made that claim in November. All that time the one obligation this government honoured is the one to give taxpayers' money to Imperial Oil and its friends. The taxpayers are not in this case the corporations; they are the same people who originally produced the wealth of Imperial Oil and its friends. That system is falling down around the ears of the Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance, and around the ears of the Leader of the Opposition and members on his front benches who have admitted publicly that they have no alternative policies and no alternative to high interest rates. They will not lift a finger to cut the profits of the banks or the oil companies who funded their election campaigns. In fact, they are racing each other to give them more. They have only one solution to the problem they created with their huge giveaway of the working people's taxes: cut the workers' pay. Of course, the Minister of Finance told us in the last couple of days that he really does not want to legislate a wage freeze. Well, all you have to remember is the election campaign of 1974 when the Prime Minister ridiculed the idea of a wage freeze and won back his majority government by promising not to implement a wage freeze which the Conservative campaign was placing front and centre. One has to give the Conservatives credit for having been honest. They asked for a wage freeze and, had they been put in office, undoubtedly would have enacted one. But the Prime Minister promised no wage freeze and within a year he froze wages. In other words, the Liberals practise what the Tories preach. We have no reason to believe the statements of the Prime Minister or Minister of Finance when they tell us they do not have a wage freeze in mind. We have every reason to believe they are simply trying to con us, trying to lull the working people of Canada into trusting them so that overnight, as before, the Prime Minister can say we have been living beyond our means so he is going to tighten your belt. He will not tighten the belts of the oil companies or the banks; he will tighten the belts of the people who produce the wealth of this country.
There is a steady campaign, Mr. Speaker, headed by this government, to misrepresent and vilify the working people of Canada. At every point the government ignores the question of profits and points incessantly at wages and salaries as the cause of our economic troubles. The Governor of the Bank of Canada, just after he received his fat raise to $104,000, made a speech in which he said the minimum wage is one of the causes of inflation. He condemns a worker who wants to get $3 an hour for his work as being a cause of inflation. This government is being forced from bad to worse by its absolute adherence and loyalty to the corporate welfare bums. We have the pathetic spectacle of the former President of El Salvador, Napoleon Duarte, lamenting that his friends in El Salvador's assembly, elected in a fraudulent vote, and his friends in Washington who helped do it, have wiped out the land reform
