In spite of his brilliance, the Prime Minister of this country will go down in history as a failure. Like the unfortunate President of El Salvador, the Prime Minister has sold our country to people who do not care about Canada, most of whom do not live here and do not care two hoots who starves to death in Canada, and he will go down in history as an enemy of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I spoke rather extensively on this bill during second reading so it is not my intention to do so again this afternoon. However, I want to make a couple of points. First of all, the $2 billion rebate to the oil and gas industry which was just recently announced is not sufficient to restore confidence in the industry, particularly on provincial lands. Something more is necessary.
A lady came to see me in my constituency office over the weekend. She told me that several years ago the governments of this nation offered working Canadians the possibility for equity investment in the oil and gas industry. In particular she mentioned the Alberta Gas Trunk Line which is now the Nova Corporation. Every Albertan was given the opportunity for equity investment in that corporation, in the tremendous growth of the oil and gas industry in Alberta. She also mentioned the Alberta energy company in which Albertans were given the opportunity for equity investment.
What I want to touch on briefly is the need for equity investment in our nation to get our economy moving. Right now Canada is sustaining itself primarily on debt investment. Debt investment creates a tremendous burden on small corporations and even on large corporations. For example, it was stated recently that the debt servicing of most companies in relation to net income went up from somewhere around 25 per cent to something like 66 per cent per annum.
Our economy is in real difficulty because of the fact that capital investment today is debt capital. Because interest rates are very high, a tremendous burden is placed on all areas of the business cycle, from the smallest corporation to the largest corporation.
The lady who came to visit me asked me when Canada would be getting round to permitting the working people of Canada to invest on an equity basis in Canadian industry instead of providing, literally, all the incentives for them to put their money into bonds, bank accounts and debt equities, through which they can gain a substantive amount of interest.
I told her that I would come back to this House and try to put a resolution before it in that connection. Under the provisions of Standing Order 43, today I moved, the following:
Madam Speaker, equity investment pessimism is pervasive in Canada. Canadians are investing their money outside of Canada and in high-interestbearing bonds and certificates. This has substantively curtailed the ability for equity capital generation in Canada and has jeopardized the survival of small business in Canada because of the high cost of debt capital. A new budget is necessary to create confidence in the Canadian economy, and it must contain incentives for equity investment. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That any new budget abolish capital gains taxation on all equity investment
in Canadian registered companies.
Because this is a taxation bill and because we are dealing with the energy industry, which industry needs other incentives today just as so many industries do too, I want to touch on the matter of abolishing capital gains. Capital gains taxation netted the federal government, both from a personal and corporate point of view, $195 million in 1975, $275 million in 1976, $320 million in 1977 and $450 million in 1978. 1 do not have the intervening figures for the last couple of years because they are still being worked on, but today the stock market has reached a new low.
Let me say that for the next several years the capital gains taxation process at the federal level will collect very few dollars because losses will be extremely high in every aspect of Canadian society this year and the next several years. If there ever was a time to use the capital gains regime to create some investor confidence, particularly in the equity market, it is today. If there ever was a time to use this tool, it should be used today because it would cost the government very little in terms of generated revenue. It is a tax that will have a very slight effect on the collection of revenues in the next several years, as the cost of collection almost exceeds what is collected. Therefore, it can be used justifiably as an incentive for growth and equity investment.
I would recommend strongly that the federal government look very seriously at the removal of capital gains taxation as an incentive for equity investment and therefore growth of the Canadian market. This will keep Canadian dollars in Canada for investment in Canada on an equity basis rather than investment as debt capital.
I want to make a point again for the second time which has to do with this energy legislation. It is the same point that I made before in connection with the Canadianization of the industry, particularly Canadianization on provincial lands. As I have said, 1 do not have any difficulty with the federal government moving substantively into the area of Canadianization of the oil and gas industry on Canadian lands where there is a single jurisdiction. But I have increasing difficulty with a policy initiated at the federal level, which is then thrust upon the provinces, having to do with provincial resources in order to Canadianize those resources.
I say again to the government that it should consider very seriously whether it wishes to extend this Canadianization program in a substantive way as it has done with the oil and

gas industry on provincial lands. This, more than any other aspect of this energy legislation, is causing instability. It is causing pessimism. It is the antithesis of good equity investment. I suggest that the federal government should think seriously of whether it really wants to force its ideological direction on Canadianization on the corporate structure on provincial lands. I say again that I have no difficulty in doing it where there is a single jurisdiction with regard to Canadian lands. But when it comes to provincial lands, it is a retardant for the regeneration of the economy. I suggest the federal government re-examine its position.
There are many other areas of this legislation about which I could speak. I spoke extensively when we debated the principle of the legislation so I will not go into that again, except to say that the Canadian economy has to be revitalized at the earliest opportunity or we will slide into a level of recession or depression not known since the 1930s. I think some stimulative measures have to be taken at the earliest possible date, stimulative measures in the area of equity investment and not debt investment.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks to add to those I made on the petroleum incentives program and the Canadian ownership rate or so-called COR program. I indicated yesterday my guess is that this program may last for two years and that then it will simply collapse.
It will collapse, first, because of the political pressures that will be brought to bear having to do with the grants. As the New Democratic Party members continually demonstrate, they cannot draw the distinction between the taxes and grants. They conclude somehow that therefore this grant program represents an extraordinary gift to the oil industry and that the pressures in that regard will be tremendous. That simple-minded approach, unfortunately, is going to be frequently heard in this House, resulting in sufficient pressure, I think, to weaken this program very substantially.
Second, the red tape associated with this program, the incredibly complex regulations and applications forms necessary to fulfil the goals of this program, are just so horrendous that the administrative cost and the difficulty of handling this program are also going to contribute to its demise.
There is also a third reason, Mr. Speaker. The third reason is that we were given testimony by the Canadian Bar Association that this program is in violation of the new charter of rights. It is in violation of the Constitution of Canada. The Canadian Bar Association gave two arguments why it is in violation. First, the recipients of the grant program, in order to receive the maximum, must be resident Canadians. As the Canadian Bar Association points out, there is no provision in the charter of rights to distinguish between Canadians on the ground of residency. That is the effect of this program-a Canadian is a Canadian. There is no way legally to distinguish between them, yet this bill tries to do so.
Second, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Bar Association points out that the program may be in violation of the charter of rights because of the freedom of association the charter guarantees. The grants provided under the PIP portion, based on the Canadian ownership rate portion, are given to corporations whose degree of Canadian ownership is at a sufficient level. In reality, a corporation is but a piece of paper; it exists for the benefit of its shareholders. What the act would do is say that if you, as a Canadian, associated yourself with shareholders who in aggregate represent more than 75 per cent of the shareholders of that corporation, then you are eligible for a grant. But if you associate with shareholders who in aggregate do not represent more than 75 per cent of the shareholders of the corporation, then you are not eligible. Therefore, this program discriminates in regard to the types of associations that Canadians are part of. The Canadian Bar Association has pointed out that this is in violation of the Canadian charter of rights.

We are not going to spend a great deal of time debating this portion of the bill, Mr. Speaker. The government has brought in some 15 amendments to try to improve a piece of trash. The effort is probably wasted because the whole thing will collapse within a year or two. In the meantime, the country will have lost untold billions of dollars, tens of thousands of jobs and the credibility of the government will have suffered. That will be the sum total of this little exercise dreamed up by that group of bright PhDs who sat down, in total ignorance of the Canadian industry, to design this program. They have wasted billions of dollars of this country's money and have wreaked havoc on the industry. That is a sad situation. Any reasonable person would suggest we need changes to prevent that kind of uncontrolled, bureaucratic stupidity from damaging the country in this way in the future.
That having been said, we do not have any particular problems with the amendments proposed by the government. Motion No. 16, which appears at our insistence, provides for judicial review of arbitrary decisions, so we are in favour of that. I think the government has put a new coat of paint on an old jalopy that will come to a grinding halt within a year or two anyway.

I had the honour, Mr. Speaker, to sit on the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation for some six weeks. I believe our party represented the Canadian public extremely well in that period. We did not accomplish what we would have liked, which was basically to abolish the bills altogether, but we did accomplish small points, one of which had to do with Bill C-104 and the amendment concerning judicial review.
During our hearings on this bill we were told so often that we did not need any special clause in here because this was provided for under the Federal Court Act. Finally they relented and gave in to judicial review. The reason we were pushing for that is very simple. These bills give the minister the most unbelievable authority to do whatever he wants, when he wants, without any discussion in Parliament. The serious fear we had was that the House of Commons was losing importance. We were frightened and scared. We deal so often with dictatorial rule, and this bill was giving too much power to any minister. At one point we referred to the fact that perhaps we might get a worse minister than we have now, although I personally could not imagine a worse minister than the one we have right now. It was something we were and are frightened of. It gives total control to the minister, but thank heavens there was some common sense in the Ministry of Justice, through the gentleman that represented that department, which allowed us to get that phrase back in.
What we are talking about in the bill and its amendments, Mr. Speaker, is an attempt to replace tax incentives with PIP grants. The government also has in this bill what is called COR, which refers to the Canadian ownership rate. All 1 can say is that these PIP grants, based on COR, have effectively removed in excess of $8 billion of investment from Canada.
Gulf Canada appeared before the committee and I asked them whether they ever considered breaking their corporation down so they could have a 50 per cent or greater Canadian ownership. 1 asked the same thing of Texaco, only I phrased it a little differently. 1 said that perhaps they should go back and re-incorporate McCall Frontenac, which was one of the first
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
companies they bought, and provide Canadian ownership in that way. They explained to me very simply that it did not really matter how it was done, but it would not work in their situation because this government was determined to remove that multinational expertise in finding oil in this country.
In the second part of this bill is the heading "Canada lands". What are PIP grants doing? They are taking funds directly out of provincial coffers and putting them toward Canada lands. Canada lands can best be described as the Beaufort Sea and the offshore, which we now refer to as Sable Island and Hibernia. The minister has made a fatal mistake in this program. He has put so much emphasis on the fact that we will become oil self-sufficient through those two areas that the cash flow has been removed from the balance of the industry which would develop traditional oil fields. The megaprojects have also been killed. You might challenge me on that, Mr. Speaker, because this bill has removed the tax incentives and the cash flow and thus eliminated the megaprojects.
I asked the chairman of Imperial Oil why his company suspended the Cold Lake project. His answer was: "Because of the National Energy Program." The same question was asked of Gulf Canada and we were given the same answer. Texaco was asked why that company was not going into the Beaufort Sea and the North Sea. Texaco is concerned because it does not feel the investment is worth the return it would get. Representatives of Home Oil were asked questions. They said Home had only one option. Home is Canadian owned and receives 80 cents on every dollar of investment. But Home's representatives told us that even with 80 cents on every dollar, and even if Home finds immense pools of oil, in 1990 it will still cost $100 a barrel to bring the product onshore. In the minister's review 1 believe the maximum price is $72, but he has dropped that amount for 1990.
He zeroed in on one single potential that we have in this country, and I am referring to the frontier and the offshore. The megaprojects have been destroyed. We have destroyed drilling in the west on traditional lands. We have removed the incentive from the oil industry. Let me just give you an example. 1 have been challenged about this in committee, but I have the figures which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) says he uses. These are his figures. They are very simple. On May 25, 1982, there were 110 drilling rigs operating in the west. On May 26, 1981, there were 250 drilling rigs operating. That tells you what these PIP grants are doing, and PIP grants can still be obtained retroactively. One hundred and forty out of 250 drilling rigs have gone. Over 60 per cent of the operating drilling rigs in the west have left. This bill is not going to fly, it is going to destroy Canada.
In the committee hearings in April, I said that 70 drilling rigs were operating, but I was told at that time by one of the brilliant men in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources that my figures were wrong and really there were

June 9, 1982
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
370 rigs operating. 1 got a copy of Oilweek and brought it to the committee hearings and showed the evidence that 70 drilling rigs were operating. The PIP grants themselves have done only one thing. They have removed the need for geologists in Canada and instead have created a tremendous need for accountants and lawyers.
I do not know if any hon. members in this House have reviewed the forms-I see one who has-which everyone has to sign to get these PIP grants. There are 27 forms involved. Let me explain what happens. Under this legislation, if there are 24 different corporations involved in one well, those 24 corporations have to file 27 returns. That to me is super bureaucracy. Think of the people we can employ reading forms and think of the people we can employ to fill in those forms!
IPAC represents the small oil companies in Canada and the Canadian Petroleum Association represents a group of larger Canadian companies and both associations appeared before our committee hearings. Representatives of those associations told us that the PIP grants will not solve our problem, but when an 11 per cent or 12 per cent PGRT is levied-and thank goodness the IORT has been removed-together with other taxes that have been imposed on the industry, there is no cash flow left. It is fine to get a PIP grant of 35 per cent in the west if you are 75 per cent Canadian owned, but if there is no cash flow the company cannot apply for this grant because the company cannot afford to borrow 65 per cent of the cost of drilling a well at 18 per cent from the bank.
This bill is an abomination. 1 think there are certain points in it that are prejudicial to Canadian citizens. I am referring to pension funds that have been invested in such companies as Imperial Oil, Gulf and Texaco. Those pension funds have
invested people's money and because those companies are American controlled there is no PIP grant available for a traditional oil field, or 25 per cent if it is frontier or off the coast. Of that 25 per cent though, 25 per cent has to be given back to Petro-Canada. People with money in pension funds are suffering because of this bill.
Another group of people who are suffering are those who have retired and those who have moved south. Perhaps they have moved to Arizona for health reasons. Those people are hurt because they do not get any credit.
Once the government brought in this energy bill, it destroyed the market to such an extent that people could not reinvest their money because prices dropped so quickly. Dome is a prime example of that. In the United States today Dome's shares fell below $5, which caused a raft of margin calls. It is a serious situation when a company like that is driven down that far. But Dome helped itself by trying to help the Liberal government to Canadianize the industry. Dome is a fine company and I hope the government will help it out, but I hope the government is not going to help Dome the way I have been hearing it will. The government will probably lend Dome $1 billion and take a piece of the action. That proves to me what Canadianization of the oil industry is. It is nationalization and it is removing the private sector.
May I call it six o'clock?
